note: Vol. I No. 41. THE DRAW-BRIDGE BECOMES AN ADDRESS. A two-storey store-and-dwelling on South Water Street 'nearly opposite the draw-bridge' and Jones & King's store 'in Water-st., near the bridge' both hang off the same landmark, and Dr. John T. Temple lets two new four-room dwelling houses. David Carver's collection notice times itself against the end of the Indian payment, and a citizens' committee is sitting on the Polish exiles then in the town.

claims.notes: A fuller week than the 3 September list: four or five arrivals against two. The schooner Phillips, Howe master, arrives from Michigan City and clears for St. Joseph in the same week, which is the short-haul trade this port lived on; the Mariah Antonette clears for St. Joseph having arrived from Detroit a week earlier (1834-09-03, claim c010). The transcription's vessel names are among the worst-recognised text in the issue and the uncertain ones are left inside their brackets.

A two-storey building on South Water Street, nearly opposite the draw-bridge, offered as one of the best business stands in the town — so the frontage facing the bridge approach was PRIME ground in September 1834, and it carried a two-storey structure combining store and dwelling. The reconstruction models South Water Street's frontage from Wright's plat and from lot claims; this is a documented storey count and a documented use at a documented distance from a fixed point. The fuller printing a week later (1834-09-17, claim c002) adds that Rider himself was next door to the Post Office.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S LUMBER DEALER IS BEING PAID IN PROMISES, AND HE IS WAITING FOR THE INDIAN PAYMENT TO END BEFORE HE SUES. Two things for the reconstruction: the September 1834 building trade ran on credit that its principal supplier could not collect, and the annuity payment at Chicago was a fixed point in the town's calendar that even a debt notice was timed against. 'Our business has become so estranged' is quoted as printed; whether the compositor set 'estranged' for 'extended' is not decided here.

claims.notes: A CHICAGO ADVERTISEMENT THAT NAMES A STREET CHICAGO DOES NOT HAVE. The copy is dated at Chicago, 26 November 1833 — the date of the Democrat's first issue — and places the shop 'on Main-street, opposite the Tremont House'. Wright's plat has no Main Street, and the Tremont stood at Lake and Dearborn. This is NOT resolved here and nothing is built on it: either the compositor set a house name for a street name, or the town used 'Main street' colloquially for one of the platted streets, or the ad is a survivor from another town's paper. It is recorded so that the contradiction is on the board rather than quietly dropped, and the placement is kept `relative` on the Tremont House, which is the part of the address this project can actually resolve.

claims.notes: POLISH EXILES ARE IN CHICAGO IN SEPTEMBER 1834 and a committee of citizens is sitting on where in Illinois to settle them, on land donated by Congress. The town's population at the scene date is built in this project out of censuses and land records; this is a documented group of residents who appear in neither. The passage is one of the badly interleaved leader columns, so only the lines that carry the committee's own words are claimed and the rest of the circular is left unread — the coverage declaration for September covers the ISSUE, not every column of it.
